Let me now dig deeper into the substantive policy analysis. Key questions:

1. Does Prop 42 actually block Prop 40? Yes — via the conflicting measures provision and the retroactivity ban.
2. Is Prop 40 good policy? Consider: one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires residing in CA as of Jan 1, 2026. Estimated to raise ~$100B (LAO estimate?). Concerns: capital flight, valuation of private companies, legal challenges (dormant Commerce Clause, retroactivity, due process), and enforcement. Many economists and even progressive-leaning analysts have concerns. Newsom opposes. Several wealthy individuals have moved.
3. Is Prop 42 itself good policy independent of Prop 40? It permanently constitutionalizes a ban on new taxes on ownership of personal property — which could be over-broad and prevent future legislatures/voters from responding to new circumstances (e.g., AI-driven inequality, tax base erosion as economy shifts from labor income to capital). It also bans retroactive taxation, which while generally a good principle, could tie the state's hands in responding to federal changes or closing loopholes (though the measure carves out a limited exception for emergencies with a 365-day limit for statutes, not for initiatives? Let me re-read: Section 2(c) says subdivision (a) shall not apply to a tax imposed by a statute passed by the Legislature on or after Jan 1, 2026 where (1) not retroactive more than 365 days and (2) governor declares emergency... So there is a limited carve-out for legislative statutes in emergencies, but no carve-out for initiative measures — meaning voters could never enact a retroactive tax through initiative.

4. Is the claim about protecting retirement accounts truthful? There's no current proposal to tax middle-class retirement accounts; the LAO notes ownership of financial assets is not taxed. McClatchy calls it a "401(k) decoy." However, proponents argue it's preemptive protection requiring a vote of the people. Note that a constitutional amendment can itself only be changed by voters anyway — so the "protection" it provides is largely redundant with the two-thirds legislative vote requirement and the fact that any new state tax requires 2/3 legislative vote or ballot measure.

5. The measure includes an unusual "Legal Defense" provision that requires the AG to appoint independent counsel and creates a continuous General Fund appropriation. Also "Liberal Construction" clause. These provisions are designed to entrench.

6. Also, note the interaction: Prop 42's Section 1(a) prohibits "No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of..." — This could arguably affect other things, e.g., a future tax on business inventory? Business equipment personal property taxes are currently exempted by statute (there's a state subvention). Could block future taxes on intangible property.

Also, importantly — could Prop 42 block a future tax on, e.g., digital assets, or block a "mansion tax"? No, that's real property.

Another consideration: does Prop 42 potentially block local taxes? "No state law" — a local tax is enacted by local government, not state law, so probably not. But it could restrict the state from authorizing local personal property taxes.

Now — my job is to give a recommendation: yes or no. Let me gather more evidence: expert analysis (LAO, tax economists, legal scholars), and the campaign finance. Also check whether the "conflict" mechanism means voting yes on 42 kills Prop 40 — and whether Prop 40 has flaws severe enough.

Let me look at:
- LAO's fiscal estimate for Prop 40 (revenue estimates).
- Analysis by tax economists on the billionaire tax (e.g., David Gamage, who drafted it; critics like Jared Walczak of Tax Foundation).
- Legal challenges to Prop 40.
- Articles on how Prop 42 could backfire or its overbreadth (e.g., does it block taxes on unrealized gains at the state level; does it block a "personal property tax" needed to replace declining revenue).

Let me also see whether the two measures' conflict provision means that if Prop 40 passes with more votes, Prop 42 is void — so a "yes" on 42 only matters if 42 gets more yes votes than 40. That's important: voting yes on 42 while voting yes on 40 is coherent (a preference ranking). But the user asks about Prop 42 alone.

Let me research further.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.

However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. Also consider the counterargument that Prop 42's personal property ban is extremely broad — "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including ... personal belongings". That means California could never, e.g., impose a new tax on boats, aircraft, or personal belongings (though local property taxes on business equipment exist). Also could prevent a tax on intangible property such as a financial transactions tax? Hmm, a financial transaction tax is a tax on a transaction, not ownership, so probably allowed. Also, the retroactivity ban would prevent future measures from doing anything retroactive — including possibly beneficial corrections? No, it only prohibits tax liability based on past conduct.

One important consideration: the "Legal Defense" provision with continuous General Fund appropriation, and the "liberal construction" — designed to be hard to overturn. Also, Prop 42 requires that a future repeal be done by voters (constitutional amendment), so it locks in policy.

Another consideration: Prop 42 conflicts with Prop 40 in a way that means if Prop 42 gets more yes votes, Prop 40 is void entirely. Given Prop 40's polling (42-46% support, likely to fail on its own anyway), a "yes" on 42 mainly matters as insurance against the billionaire tax and as an entrenchment of the ban on personal-property/wealth taxes.

Let me also weigh: Is there a legitimate fairness argument against retroactive taxation? Prop 40 applies to residency on Jan 1, 2026 — before voters approved it in Nov 2026. That is retroactive. Retroactive taxation is generally disfavored but often upheld if brief and justified (e.g., tax changes effective at start of tax year are common — many tax changes apply to the whole tax year even if enacted mid-year; e.g., California's 2012 Prop 30 raised income tax rates retroactively to Jan 1, 2012!). That's an important fact: Prop 30 (2012) applied retroactively to the beginning of the tax year. So a blanket constitutional ban on retroactivity could have prevented Prop 30-style measures — which are common tools to address mid-year fiscal shortfalls. Prop 42 does carve out an exception for legislative statutes with a fiscal emergency declaration and ≤365-day retroactivity, but NOT for initiatives. So a future voter-approved initiative like Prop 30 (2012) — which was a legislative constitutional amendment, not an initiative — hmm, Prop 30 was placed on ballot by the Legislature. Prop 42's ban covers "no state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026" for the retroactivity ban, but the carve-out in 2(c) applies only to "a tax imposed by a statute passed by the Legislature". So legislative constitutional amendments and initiatives would not have the emergency carve-out? Actually for the retroactivity provision, the ban applies to state laws and constitutional provisions; the exception is only for statutes passed by the Legislature. So a future legislative constitutional amendment or initiative that imposed a retroactive tax would be barred entirely. Hmm, wait: if the ban applies to "provision of this Constitution enacted on or after Jan 1 2026", then a later constitutional amendment could... Actually, a later constitutional amendment could amend Prop 42 itself — but Article VIII new sections would need to comply; however, the people retain power to amend the constitution, and later amendments generally prevail over earlier conflicting ones (last in time). So Prop 42 could be repealed or amended by a future ballot measure approved by voters. It's not truly permanent. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.

It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Another consideration: Prop 42 Section 1(a) prohibits taxes on "ownership or control" of personal property. Could this affect the state's ability to impose an annual tax on... e.g., a tax on boats/aircraft (currently taxed as personal property by counties under Prop 13 — local, not state, and existing). What about a future "split-roll"? That's real property.

Also — could Prop 42 bar a tax on the ownership of firearms? Ammunition tax is an excise tax on sale. A tax on gun ownership would be barred. Hmm, interesting but not central.

Also relevant: would Prop 42 prohibit a future state tax on cryptocurrency/digital assets ownership? Yes. Would it prohibit a state tax on stock ownership (like a mark-to-market tax on billionaires' unrealized gains — as NY and other states have considered)? A mark-to-market income tax is arguably a tax on income from unrealized appreciation, not on "ownership" — but it's based on ownership. Legal ambiguity here is a real concern: this ambiguity might chill future tax reforms even against high earners generally, e.g., California's proposal to tax unrealized gains (AB 1927? there was a proposal in 2025 to tax billionaires' unrealized gains). Actually there's the "2026 Billionaire Tax Act" plus proposals from Assemblymember Alex Lee for wealth taxes. Prop 42 would block all of them permanently unless repealed by voters.

Now, a key question for me as the assistant: what should the user vote? I need to come to a decision — yes or no — and provide reasoning. Let me weigh things carefully, and gather a bit more evidence, particularly:

1. Whether Prop 42's claims are misleading (401(k) protection). Verified: California doesn't tax retirement account ownership; Prop 40 excludes qualified retirement accounts and pensions; the "six proposals" claim — SF Chronicle says lawmakers killed all six wealth tax proposals since 2019; those targeted the rich, not 401(k)s. So the "protect your retirement" framing is largely a decoy.

2. Whether the retroactivity ban has independent merit. Retroactive taxation is disfavored, but modest retroactivity (to Jan 1 of the same year) is a common, legal legislative tool (e.g., Prop 30 in 2012, and tax changes effective retroactively to the start of the tax year). Prop 42's ban is absolute for initiatives, and for legislative statutes only allows up to 365 days in declared emergencies. This could hamper California's ability to conform to federal tax changes mid-year, or to close abusive tax shelters discovered mid-year. Actually many states enact retroactive conformity. The ban may create real fiscal-administration problems.

Hmm, wait. Let me re-read Section 2(a)(2): "This subdivision also applies to a tax that is imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." That's aimed at Prop 40.

3. Whether the measure entrenches itself via the Legal Defense provision (AG must appoint independent counsel with continuous General Fund appropriation). This is a notable governance red flag: it commandeers state funds and undermines the AG's authority, and it's designed to prevent the state from defending against it. Also the "liberal construction" instruction.

4. Whether it nullifies Prop 40 — yes, and this is a "poison pill" tactic. But note: such conflict provisions are common in CA initiative practice (e.g., Prop 22 in 2020 had a 7/8 amendment requirement; various measures). The LAO notes the conflict.

5. Consider the fairness/democracy angle: ~$293M-$368M from 30 billionaires to defeat Prop 40 and pass 41/42 — one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history. The measure is being sold to voters with a framing (protect your 401k) that is not accurate. Voting "no" rejects deceptive ballot-measure tactics.

6. On the other hand: is a state-level wealth tax actually bad policy? Evidence: wealth taxes have been abandoned across Europe (France, Sweden, etc.) due to capital flight and administration issues. California's income tax base is highly dependent on the ultra-wealthy (~top 1% pays ~45% of income tax; billionaires pay much). Even LAO warns of behavioral responses. Rauh/Jaros estimate net losses. Saez/Zucman estimate big revenue. Genuinely uncertain. But note: a NO vote on Prop 42 doesn't require endorsing Prop 40 — you can vote no on both. Since Prop 40 is polling below 50% and likely to fail on its own, the practical effect of voting no on 42 may be small — but if Prop 40 passes with fewer votes than 42, then 42 would kill it.

Hmm, but there's a strategic consideration: if you oppose Prop 40 and also oppose Prop 42, you vote no on both (like Mercury News and George Skelton). If you support Prop 40, you vote no on 42. The only people who should vote yes on 42 are those who want a permanent constitutional ban on personal property/wealth taxes and retroactive taxes.

So the real question: Should California permanently constitutionalize a ban on new taxes on ownership of personal property (including all intangible assets, business interests, IP, digital assets) and on retroactive taxation?

Considerations against a permanent ban:
- Tax policy needs flexibility. As the economy shifts (AI, capital vs labor income, decline of gas tax), states may need to tax wealth/capital. California's tax system is heavily reliant on income; a ban on personal property taxes forecloses a whole category.
- The measure's definition is extremely broad — "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including ... personal belongings." This could bar even modest, widely supported taxes like an annual luxury tax on private jets/yachts, or a tax on second homes' contents? Or a tax on stock/bond ownership.
- It's a one-way ratchet: it protects existing taxes (grandfather) but bars any new ones, even if approved by 2/3 of the Legislature or by a majority of voters (unless voters first repeal Prop 42). Actually — could voters approve a new wealth tax by initiative? Prop 42 says "No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact..." A later initiative that conflicts would need to expressly repeal/amend Prop 42 — under California law, an initiative can amend another initiative if it furthers its purpose or with voter approval; and constitutional amendments by voters can supersede. So it's not truly irreversible, but it raises the bar significantly (you'd need a separate repeal measure or a measure explicitly overriding).
- The measure's stated rationale is false/misleading (no proposal to tax 401(k)s; Prop 40 explicitly excludes qualified retirement accounts and pensions).
- Funded by parties with an enormous direct financial interest; the most expensive intervention in CA ballot history.

Considerations for:
- Retroactive taxation is genuinely disfavored; Prop 40's retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026 (before the election!) is a legitimate fairness concern. But Prop 42 goes much further.
- Wealth taxes are hard to administer and cause capital flight; banning them at state level could be seen as fiscal prudence (avoids a value-destroying one-time tax). But that's an argument for voting no on Prop 40, not for a permanent constitutional ban.
- Protecting pensions/retirement from future taxation: a real, if speculative, benefit. Note however that some argue there IS a plausible path: if a wealth tax on billionaires is enacted, expanding it to millionaires later is a known pattern ("boiling frog"). But the two-thirds requirement plus political reality makes it unlikely, and voters would have to approve.

Now let's check some more facts:
- Does Prop 40 exclude retirement accounts? The SF Chronicle says Prop 40 "specifically excludes qualified pensions and retirement accounts, including 401(k)s" but includes Roth IRAs over $10M as taxable assets. Let me verify from Prop 40's text. Actually LA Times says "Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded." And the Chronicle notes Roth IRAs >$10M included. So proponents of Prop 42's claim that Prop 40 would tax your retirement is mostly false (except mega-Roth IRAs which only billionaires have).
- Also the Yes on 42 campaign ads: did they claim Prop 40 would tax middle-class retirement accounts? SEIU says they spread lies. Let me check fact-checks of Prop 42 ads.

Also, check the "6 proposals to tax retirement and savings accounts" claim — SF Chronicle says lawmakers killed all six wealth tax proposals since 2019, none targeting 401(k)s. Let's see if any fact-check addressed the Prop 42 claim.

Let me also check whether Prop 42 would block the state's ability to tax, e.g., "control" — the phrase "ownership or control" could affect trust arrangements.

Additional angle: does Prop 42 possibly conflict with federal requirements or with the state's existing tax structure? Probably not.

Another important angle: Prop 42 could block a future tax on intangible personal property of businesses — which some states are considering as the economy digitizes. Also, could it block California from participating in a multistate approach to taxing digital assets? Yes.

Let me also see whether there is any analysis suggesting Prop 42 could affect the existing vehicle license fee or business personal property taxes if they were "re-enacted" — Section 1(b) says nothing alters taxes "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025." If the Legislature later amended the VLF rate, would that be a "new" tax? Ambiguity could create litigation risk over routine tax adjustments. For example, if the state increased the vehicle license fee, is that a "tax on ownership of personal property" enacted after Jan 1, 2026? Arguably yes — the VLF is a tax on ownership of vehicles (personal property)! So Prop 42 could bar any future increase in the vehicle license fee, or any new local/state tax on vehicles, boats, aircraft, business equipment. That's a much bigger deal than most voters realize: VLF increases have historically been used (and are a classic revenue tool). Also, the state could no longer replace declining gas-tax revenue with a road-charge or vehicle-based tax — a vehicle miles traveled (VMT) fee is arguably a fee, not a tax... but a VMT tax would be based on use, not ownership, so probably fine.

Hmm, but the ban is on taxes on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — as defined in Section 3(a) to include "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including... personal belongings". A VLF is a tax on ownership of a car (personal property) — so yes, Prop 42 would bar a new state tax on vehicle ownership. Wait — but is VLF a "tax"? Article XIII A Section 3(b)... hmm, VLF is actually an in-lieu property tax; it's in the Revenue & Taxation Code and is treated as a property tax. Actually, California's VLF is characterized as an ad valorem property tax on vehicles (personal property). So Prop 42 would prohibit new state VLF-type taxes. Also counties' business personal property taxes are local, not state, and existing.

That's a meaningful consequence: it forecloses taxing vehicles/boats/aircraft/business equipment — the classic personal property tax base — at the state level, and could also restrict the state's ability to authorize new local personal property taxes.

Let me verify with expert commentary. Let me search for analyses discussing what Prop 42 would block beyond wealth taxes (e.g., VLF, luxury taxes).

Also let me check the CalMatters article on Newsom's endorsement and any "what matters" explainer.

Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Newsom has not yet taken a position on Prop. 41, another Brin-backed, anti-billionaire tax measure that would nullify Prop. 40 by subjecting the tax revenues to certain state spending limits and audits, said spokesperson Izzy Gardon. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. Sign up for free Δ But he has also sought to take advantage this year of a populist upswing (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/) and frustration toward tech billionaires ahead of his decision on whether to run for president after he leaves office. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments. # Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.*** Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Newsom has not yet taken a position on Prop. 41, another Brin-backed, anti-billionaire tax measure that would nullify Prop. 40 by subjecting the tax revenues to certain state spending limits and audits, said spokesperson Izzy Gardon. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments. 6. On the other hand: is a state-level wealth tax actually bad policy? Evidence: wealth taxes have been abandoned across Europe (France, Sweden, etc.) due to capital flight and administration issues. California's income tax base is highly dependent on the ultra-wealthy (~top 1% pays ~45% of income tax; billionaires pay much). Even LAO warns of behavioral responses. Rauh/Jaros estimate net losses. Saez/Zucman estimate big revenue. Genuinely uncertain. But note: a NO vote on Prop 42 doesn't require endorsing Prop 40 — you can vote no on both. Since Prop 40 is polling below 50% and likely to fail on its own, the practical effect of voting no on 42 may be small — but if Prop 40 passes with fewer votes than 42, then 42 would kill it.

Hmm, but there's a strategic consideration: if you oppose Prop 40 and also oppose Prop 42, you vote no on both (like Mercury News and George Skelton). If you support Prop 40, you vote no on 42. The only people who should vote yes on 42 are those who want a permanent constitutional ban on personal property/wealth taxes and retroactive taxes.

So the real question: Should California permanently constitutionalize a ban on new taxes on ownership of personal property (including all intangible assets, business interests, IP, digital assets) and on retroactive taxation?

Considerations against a permanent ban:
- Tax policy needs flexibility. As the economy shifts (AI, capital vs labor income, decline of gas tax), states may need to tax wealth/capital. California's tax system is heavily reliant on income; a ban on personal property taxes forecloses a whole category.
- The measure's definition is extremely broad — "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including ... personal belongings." This could bar even modest, widely supported taxes like an annual luxury tax on private jets/yachts, or a tax on second homes' contents? Or a tax on stock/bond ownership.
- It's a one-way ratchet: it protects existing taxes (grandfather) but bars any new ones, even if approved by 2/3 of the Legislature or by a majority of voters (unless voters first repeal Prop 42). Actually — could voters approve a new wealth tax by initiative? Prop 42 says "No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact..." A later initiative that conflicts would need to expressly repeal/amend Prop 42 — under California law, an initiative can amend another initiative if it furthers its purpose or with voter approval; and constitutional amendments by voters can supersede. So it's not truly irreversible, but it raises the bar significantly (you'd need a separate repeal measure or a measure explicitly overriding).
- The measure's stated rationale is false/misleading (no proposal to tax 401(k)s; Prop 40 explicitly excludes qualified retirement accounts and pensions).
- Funded by parties with an enormous direct financial interest; the most expensive intervention in CA ballot history.

Considerations for:
- Retroactive taxation is genuinely disfavored; Prop 40's retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026 (before the election!) is a legitimate fairness concern. But Prop 42 goes much further.
- Wealth taxes are hard to administer and cause capital flight; banning them at state level could be seen as fiscal prudence (avoids a value-destroying one-time tax). But that's an argument for voting no on Prop 40, not for a permanent constitutional ban.
- Protecting pensions/retirement from future taxation: a real, if speculative, benefit. Note however that some argue there IS a plausible path: if a wealth tax on billionaires is enacted, expanding it to millionaires later is a known pattern ("boiling frog"). But the two-thirds requirement plus political reality makes it unlikely, and voters would have to approve.

Now let's check some more facts:
- Does Prop 40 exclude retirement accounts? The SF Chronicle says Prop 40 "specifically excludes qualified pensions and retirement accounts, including 401(k)s" but includes Roth IRAs over $10M as taxable assets. Let me verify from Prop 40's text. Actually LA Times says "Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded." And the Chronicle notes Roth IRAs >$10M included. So proponents of Prop 42's claim that Prop 40 would tax your retirement is mostly false (except mega-Roth IRAs which only billionaires have).
- Also the Yes on 42 campaign ads: did they claim Prop 40 would tax middle-class retirement accounts? SEIU says they spread lies. Let me check fact-checks of Prop 42 ads.

Also, check the "6 proposals to tax retirement and savings accounts" claim — SF Chronicle says lawmakers killed all six wealth tax proposals since 2019, none targeting 401(k)s. Let's see if any fact-check addressed the Prop 42 claim.

Let me also check whether Prop 42 would block the state's ability to tax, e.g., "control" — the phrase "ownership or control" could affect trust arrangements.

Additional angle: does Prop 42 possibly conflict with federal requirements or with the state's existing tax structure? Probably not.

Another important angle: Prop 42 could block a future tax on intangible personal property of businesses — which some states are considering as the economy digitizes. Also, could it block California from participating in a multistate approach to taxing digital assets? Yes.

Let me also see whether there is any analysis suggesting Prop 42 could affect the existing vehicle license fee or business personal property taxes if they were "re-enacted" — Section 1(b) says nothing alters taxes "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025." If the Legislature later amended the VLF rate, would that be a "new" tax? Ambiguity could create litigation risk over routine tax adjustments. For example, if the state increased the vehicle license fee, is that a "tax on ownership of personal property" enacted after Jan 1, 2026? Arguably yes — the VLF is a tax on ownership of vehicles (personal property)! So Prop 42 could bar any future increase in the vehicle license fee, or any new local/state tax on vehicles, boats, aircraft, business equipment. That's a much bigger deal than most voters realize: VLF increases have historically been used (and are a classic revenue tool). Also, the state could no longer replace declining gas-tax revenue with a road-charge or vehicle-based tax — a vehicle miles traveled (VMT) fee is arguably a fee, not a tax... but a VMT tax would be based on use, not ownership, so probably fine.

Hmm, but the ban is on taxes on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — as defined in Section 3(a) to include "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including... personal belongings". A VLF is a tax on ownership of a car (personal property) — so yes, Prop 42 would bar a new state tax on vehicle ownership. Wait — but is VLF a "tax"? Article XIII A Section 3(b)... hmm, VLF is actually an in-lieu property tax; it's in the Revenue & Taxation Code and is treated as a property tax. Actually, California's VLF is characterized as an ad valorem property tax on vehicles (personal property). So Prop 42 would prohibit new state VLF-type taxes. Also counties' business personal property taxes are local, not state, and existing.

That's a meaningful consequence: it forecloses taxing vehicles/boats/aircraft/business equipment — the classic personal property tax base — at the state level, and could also restrict the state's ability to authorize new local personal property taxes.

Let me verify with expert commentary. Let me search for analyses discussing what Prop 42 would block beyond wealth taxes (e.g., VLF, luxury taxes).

Also let me check the CalMatters article on Newsom's endorsement and any "what matters" explainer.

The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments. Gavin Newsom backs measure to kill the billionaire tax and ban future wealth taxes

By Jeanne Kuang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax, but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. 

On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. 

But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property.

If you’ve seen the ads for it, Proposition 42 might seem like a common-sense measure.
Its opponents say it’s anything but.
The tag line for the yes on 42 campaign is “protect your retirement and life savings.” In the increasingly frequent ads for the measure, everyday people such as firefighters and teachers warn that state legislators have tried to tax such savings in the past, and the law is needed to safeguard everyone’s nest eggs.
But opponents of Prop. 42 say they see it as little more than a ruse to try to kill Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax. What’s worse, they say, is that because of the way the measure is written, it could harm much more than just that.
Here’s what Prop. 42 would do, why proponents think it’s needed, and why opponents say it’s a cynical and potentially dangerous measure.
What it would do: The measure would prohibit the state from imposing a wealth tax.
Specifically, it would bar any new taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that are placed on personal property; retirement or other kinds of personal savings; investments; business interests; and other non-real estate assets. It would also forbid any tax with retroactive provisions, such as to determine whether someone was a resident prior to the tax’s effective date, enacted after the start of this year.
Prop. 42 would nullify Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/what-you-should-know-about-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax/article_e9e431c7-7577-43cf-b4fb-a0601b81c54c.html) — in the event that both pass but Prop. 42 attracts more votes.
When it would take effect: Five days after the Secretary of State certifies the election results — but it would apply to any applicable tax measures passed on or after Jan. 1 of this year.
Who would be covered by it: Ostensibly everyone in the state, but the only taxes on savings that are currently or have recently been considered are those on the wealthy — most notably, Prop. 40, which would only hit those with more than $1 billion in assets.
Who sponsored it: Reportedly, Sergey Brin (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/), the co-founder of Google, via Building a Better California (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html), the political committee he formed earlier this year (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/27/us/politics/sergey-brin-gg-soto-trump-california-billionaire-tax.html).
Why: Opponents of Prop. 42 argue Brin and Building a Better California put it and Prop. 41 on the ballot specifically to stymie the billionaire tax. While ostensibly being about other things, both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 include the same provision that would nullify Prop. 40 — even if it passes — should either one get more votes.
Reporting in The New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html) and CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) has backed up opponents’ assertions about that being the real motivation behind Prop. 42.
But earlier this year, Nathan Click, a spokesman for the yes on 42 campaign, denied that the measure was intended as a response to the billionaire-tax proposal. Instead, he said, Prop. 42 was designed to protect Californians’ retirement savings in the wake of efforts to tax them.
California’s Constitution allows such savings to be taxed, Prop. 42 proponents argue. In recent years, California legislators have proposed five different bills or constitutional amendments — not including Prop. 40 — that would have done just that, the campaign backing it points out on its website.
To be clear, all of those efforts, including Prop. 40, would have taxed wealthy residents; no one who had less than $15 million in assets would have had their retirement savings taxed under any of those measures, and all but one focused on those with at least $500 million in assets.
That said, Click said Prop. 42 was motivated by the fact that other tax policies in the past that were designed to be temporary or only hit richer people have been made permanent or extended to cover more of the populace.
Supporters: Building a Better California, the political committee that has gotten almost all of its funding from Brin and other billionaires (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/billionaire-tax-fight-has-become-200m-battle/article_31b8898d-bb5a-4ff5-97a0-5921537adea6.html). Politicians and political groups including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Republican Party. Business groups including the state and various local and ethnic chambers of commerce. Public-safety groups including the California Professional Firefighters and the California Association of Highway Patrolmen. Labor groups such as the State Building & Construction Trades Council and the California State Council of Laborers. Antitax groups such as the state and several local taxpayers associations.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (seen in San Francisco on Friday) has expressed opposition to Prop. 40 and support for Prop. 42.

Opponents: Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union that sponsored Prop. 40. Other labor groups, including the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFSCME California and United Teachers Los Angeles. Political groups including the California Democratic Party, California DSA and Working Families Party. Elected officials such as Rep. Ro Khanna, Assemblymember Alex Lee and U.S. Sen. Arguments against it: Opponents say any arguments made in favor of Prop. 42 are just pretext.
