Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Now I have a fairly comprehensive picture. Let me also check the SSRN report by Galle/Gamage/Shanske to verify claims about Prop 42 threatening Medi-Cal hospital taxes and Prop 3. And check whether there's any counter-analysis from a neutral legal expert about Prop 42's scope (e.g., does it bar vehicle license fee increases? Does it affect local taxes? SPUR says it prohibits new state AND local taxes on personal property — hmm, SPUR says "state and local" but the text says "no state law"). Actually SPUR's summary claims local too, but the text limits to state law. However, "no state law ... may ... authorize collection of a tax" — so the state could not authorize local governments to impose new personal property taxes. That effectively restricts local options too (since local taxes require state authorization).

Let me verify the Galle et al. report claims and see if there's a rebuttal from the Yes campaign or from neutral tax experts (e.g., from the Tax Foundation, or from law professors like Darien Shanske is on the Prop 40 side; who's neutral?). Maybe there's a piece from CalMatters' "how the billionaire tax could be defeated" that explains the mechanics.

Also relevant: whether Prop 42 could be a problem for the state's ability to comply with future federal requirements or to tax things like a "stock transfer tax"? Hmm.

Let me also weigh: Is the retroactivity ban actually harmful? Many tax policies use modest retroactivity (to Jan 1 of the tax year). Prop 42's exception only applies to statutes passed by the Legislature with a declared emergency, ≤365 days. So routine year-start retroactivity would be barred unless there's an emergency declaration. E.g., California conforms to federal tax code changes retroactively to Jan 1 sometimes. Would Prop 42 bar retroactive conformity? Conformity generally changes the tax base, not creating a new tax... but "tax liability based on conduct/activities prior to effective date" — a retroactive rate increase would be barred. This could hamper mid-year revenue solutions (which California has used, e.g., 2009 furloughs/Prop 1A in 2009 raised taxes retroactively to Jan 1, 2009; Prop 30 in 2012 applied retroactively to Jan 1, 2012). Notably, Prop 30 (2012) was approved by voters in November and applied to the entire 2012 tax year — retroactive. Under Prop 42, a similar measure in the future would be barred (since it's a constitutional amendment placed by the Legislature, and the exception covers only statutes). That's a concrete, real example of collateral damage: Prop 30-style mid-year fiscal rescues would be unconstitutional. That's a meaningful argument against Prop 42.

Let me verify that Prop 30 (2012) was retroactive to Jan 1, 2012. Yes — Prop 30 temporarily raised the sales tax by 0.25% effective Jan 1, 2013? Hmm. Let me check: Prop 30 increased the state sales and use tax by one-quarter cent, effective... I recall Prop 30's income tax increases applied to tax year 2012 (retroactive to January 1, 2012), and the sales tax increase began January 1, 2013. Yes: Prop 30 raised income tax rates retroactively for the 2012 tax year (approved Nov 6, 2012). So a future Prop 30-type measure would be barred by Prop 42 (as an initiative or LCA — the exception only covers statutes). Good example. Let me verify quickly.

Also the 2009 budget deal / Prop 1A? Not needed.

Let me verify Prop 30 retroactivity and also look for the Galle/Gamage/Shanske report on SSRN. Additionally, check the League of Women Voters position and any other "good government" groups.

Also check whether the Yes on 42 campaign made misleading claims in ads — e.g., ads implying Prop 40 would tax your 401(k). Fact-checks: CalMatters says Prop 40 excludes most retirement accounts; only Roth IRAs >$10M counted. The Examiner says all the five legislative proposals targeted those with $15M+ or $500M+ assets. So the "protect your retirement" claim is misleading in that no existing proposal targets ordinary retirement savings.

Let me do two more fetches: Prop 30 retroactivity check and the SSRN report.

1. Is there any credible neutral/legal analysis defending Prop 42's drafting? The Yes campaign (Nathan Click) says the Galle claims are "total BS." The Galle memo mentions "threats to the health plan and hospital taxes that currently help fund Medi-Cal" — but under Prop 42 existing taxes are grandfathered; the threat would be to future re-authorization of the MCO tax (which expires and requires periodic legislative renewal — the MCO tax was extended in 2023 through 2026, needing renewal!). That's a serious collateral concern: the managed care organization tax is periodically re-enacted; if a re-enactment after Jan 1, 2026 counts as a "new" tax... but the MCO tax is on gross receipts, not on ownership of personal property. Hmm, unless it's considered retroactive? MCO tax extensions typically apply prospectively. Let me check the Galle memo detail to see what specifically they claim about hospital/health plan taxes — maybe it's about Prop 41's Gann limit provision, not Prop 42. Actually reading the TaxProf excerpt: "the deceptive language of Props 41 and 42 could threaten much more than just Prop 40—including threats to the health plan and hospital taxes that currently help fund Medi-Cal." Let me look at the memo (scholarship.law.missouri.edu) to see the specifics.

3. Also consider Prop 42's effect on Prop 3 (making the high-earner income tax rates permanent). Galle et al. say it "could be read to nullify Prop 3" — because Prop 3 would make permanent rates that expire in 2030 (a new constitutional provision enacted after Jan 1, 2026 taxing capital gains = arguably a tax on personal property and/or retroactive). The Yes campaign denies this. That's a genuine legal ambiguity that creates risk: litigation could jeopardize Prop 3, which funds schools and mental health services. However, note that Prop 3 is a legislative constitutional amendment extending existing rates, and Prop 42's Section 1(b) says nothing alters taxes "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025" — the existing 12.3%/13.3% rates are in effect and were first collected before then, so extending them likely falls within the grandfather. Also capital gains tax is a tax on income from realization, not on "ownership or control." So the Galle claim seems legally weak (proponents call it BS). But it does illustrate drafting ambiguity risk. I should weigh this appropriately — it's contested.

Let me quickly check the Missouri memo for its specific claims about Prop 42 and the health plan/hospital taxes, to assess credibility.

4. Another consideration: Prop 42's Section 4 says "This article applies to all statewide initiative measures submitted to the electors on or after January 1, 2026, including measures that appear on the ballot at the same election" — meaning it reaches back to cover Prop 40 (submitted to electors Nov 2026). Fine.

5. What about the possibility that Prop 42 blocks future taxes on personal property that could be progressive tools — e.g., a tax on second homes' contents? Or a tax on private jets? Or the state's ability to help localities fund services by authorizing a local tax on intangible property? SPUR says it constrains local and state governments' ability to raise revenue for housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services. Hmm — the measure says "no state law... may authorize collection of a tax", which would bar state authorization of new local personal property taxes. Also, California's sales tax base could shift to services; not personal property ownership.

Consideration: Would Prop 42 bar a future tax on business inventory or business equipment at the state level? Yes — new ones. Currently business equipment is taxed locally (with a state subvention). If the state wanted to repeal the welfare exemption for machinery... that's existing.

6. Weighing whether the retroactivity ban is good policy on its own: There's a legitimate fairness argument. But blanket constitutional bans on retroactivity are unusual; and the measure's emergency carve-out is narrow (only statutes, only ≤365 days, only with declared emergency, only for Legislature — not for initiatives or LCAs). This blocks Prop 30-style mid-year fiscal rescue measures that voters approved in the past. Also, modest retroactivity to the beginning of the tax year is a standard, court-approved tool (US Supreme Court, United States v. Carlton, 1994, upheld retroactive estate tax provision; and the CA example of Prop 30).

Hmm, note the SF Chronicle cited a 1993 case (Carlton was 1994; the 1993 one might be "United States v. Darusmont"? Actually the Chronicle said the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 that retroactive taxes can be constitutional — that's likely Carlton (1994) or "Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp v. R.A. Gray" (1984). Whatever.)

7. What about the fiscal impact? LAO: "Possibility that tax revenues will be lower in the future... unclear." So the direct fiscal impact is uncertain.

8. Democratic process consideration: Prop 42 is a "poison pill" designed to nullify another initiative that voters may approve. Under California law, when two conflicting initiatives both pass, the one with more votes prevails — that's the standard constitutional rule (Art. II, §10(b)). Prop 42's conflict clause mirrors this rule for the most part. But its "self-executing revival" clause (if the conflicting measure is later held invalid, Prop 42 revives) is unusual.

Actually, an important nuance: Prop 42's conflict clause says if Prop 42 receives a greater number of affirmative votes, "all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void" — that's consistent with existing law. But there's a subtlety: Prop 42 would prevail in its entirety even if only parts conflict. Also Prop 42 applies to "all statewide initiative measures submitted to the electors on or after January 1, 2026" — meaning it could theoretically nullify other initiatives on the same ballot (like Prop 3?) if deemed conflicting. Hmm, the conflict clause (Sec. 5) is limited to measures that impose taxes on personal property or retroactive taxes. Prop 3 arguably extends income taxes on capital gains — Galle says it "could be read" to conflict. Risk of litigation over Prop 3.

Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California Public Finance (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2381&context=facpubs)
Authors
David Gamage , University of Missouri School of Law (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22David%20Gamage%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Brian D. Galle (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22Brian%20D.%20Galle%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Darien Shanske (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22Darien%20Shanske%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Document Type
Article
Publication Date
9-2026
Abstract
This memorandum discusses the possible collateral damage that Propositions 41 and 42 (on the ballot in California on November 3, 2026) might cause. The two propositions were concocted very quickly by billionaires in order to trick voters that will vote for Proposition 40 (the billionaire tax) also to vote for these propositions that are designed to undermine the billionaire tax.
The basic trick is that these propositions have plausible seeming veneers but hide a poison pill that aims to frustrate the functioning of the billionaire tax. The veneers are “plausible seeming” because they address problems that are not problems. For example, Prop 42 protects retirement assets when there is no threat to them – certainly not from Prop 40 (which exempts them).
But this memo focuses on an issue other than their deceptiveness and general disrespect for the democratic process. Because these propositions were drafted so quickly and poorly as poison pills for one tax measure, they could, if passed, impact many other vital policy initiatives. Some possible negative impacts include.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners) or invalidate it outright.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have many employees on Medi-Cal.
· The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or otherwise.
· The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for financing a wide array of local services.

(2026).

Abstract
This memorandum discusses the possible collateral damage that Propositions 41 and 42 (on the ballot in California on November 3, 2026) might cause. The two propositions were concocted very quickly by billionaires in order to trick voters that will vote for Proposition 40 (the billionaire tax) also to vote for these propositions that are designed to undermine the billionaire tax.
The basic trick is that these propositions have plausible seeming veneers but hide a poison pill that aims to frustrate the functioning of the billionaire tax. The veneers are “plausible seeming” because they address problems that are not problems. For example, Prop 42 protects retirement assets when there is no threat to them – certainly not from Prop 40 (which exempts them).
But this memo focuses on an issue other than their deceptiveness and general disrespect for the democratic process. Because these propositions were drafted so quickly and poorly as poison pills for one tax measure, they could, if passed, impact many other vital policy initiatives. Some possible negative impacts include.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners) or invalidate it outright.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have many employees on Medi-Cal.
· The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or otherwise.
· The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for financing a wide array of local services.

A VMT fee is a fee based on miles driven (use), not ownership — probably OK. But an increase in the vehicle license fee (ownership-based) would be barred. That's a real constraint.

Let me verify the Galle memo's specific claims about Prop 42 (e.g., VLF, Medi-Cal taxes) by fetching the Missouri scholarship page or the SSRN PDF. Also check the League of Women Voters and other nonpartisan orgs. And check the California Chamber of Commerce / CalTax positions (they support). Let me do a couple more fetches, then decide.

Actually, let me also verify one thing: whether Prop 42 might bar a future state estate/inheritance tax (a tax on transfer at death). Section 1(a) bars taxes on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — an estate tax is imposed on the transfer of a decedent's estate, arguably on "control"/ownership at death. There's ambiguity. An estate tax is a policy option some states use; California has considered reinstating one. Prop 42 could complicate that. Also, the retroactivity ban would bar any retroactive estate tax.

Authors
David Gamage , University of Missouri School of Law (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22David%20Gamage%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Brian D. Galle (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22Brian%20D.%20Galle%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Darien Shanske (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/do/search/?q=author%3A%22Darien%20Shanske%22&start=0&context=3478732)
Document Type
Article
Publication Date
9-2026
Abstract
This memorandum discusses the possible collateral damage that Propositions 41 and 42 (on the ballot in California on November 3, 2026) might cause. The two propositions were concocted very quickly by billionaires in order to trick voters that will vote for Proposition 40 (the billionaire tax) also to vote for these propositions that are designed to undermine the billionaire tax.
The basic trick is that these propositions have plausible seeming veneers but hide a poison pill that aims to frustrate the functioning of the billionaire tax. The veneers are “plausible seeming” because they address problems that are not problems. For example, Prop 42 protects retirement assets when there is no threat to them – certainly not from Prop 40 (which exempts them).
But this memo focuses on an issue other than their deceptiveness and general disrespect for the democratic process. Because these propositions were drafted so quickly and poorly as poison pills for one tax measure, they could, if passed, impact many other vital policy initiatives. Some possible negative impacts include.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners) or invalidate it outright.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have many employees on Medi-Cal.
· The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or otherwise.
· The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for financing a wide array of local services.

I now have a very solid picture. Let me do a couple more checks for balance:

1. Verify the Yes campaign's claim of "five or six legislative proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts" — the Examiner said all five targeted those with $15M+/$500M+ assets. That's fact-checked enough.

2. Check whether there's a strong conservative/libertarian case that Prop 42 is good policy regardless (e.g., Tax Foundation, CalTax, Howard Jarvis). OC Register and LA Daily News endorsed Yes. Let me quickly check the Tax Foundation's view on Prop 42 and Prop 40 for balance. Also let me consider the "capital flight" evidence more concretely: how many billionaires left CA; did the state lose revenue? LAO says < $1B/yr losses. Rauh says much bigger. Also, the exodus already happened regardless of outcome — a "yes" on 42 might signal California won't do wealth taxes, possibly encouraging return? Speculative.

3. One more consideration: if Prop 40 fails (likely per polls), Prop 42 still passes/fails on its own — and if it passes, it entrenches the ban. So the decision is essentially about whether to entrench the ban.

Let me quickly check the Tax Foundation's analysis of Prop 40/42 for a counterweight, then finalize.

Actually, I have enough. But one more thing worth checking: whether Prop 42's language could be interpreted to bar a state estate tax or a tax on unrealized capital gains (mark-to-market) — the Galle memo says it "could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income." That's contested by the Yes campaign but shows ambiguity risk. Also the possibility it interferes with the Vehicle License Fee reform.

Also: does Prop 42 apply to local taxes? LWV says new state taxes; SPUR says state and local. Text says "no state law ... may authorize collection of a tax on the ownership..." — so it restricts state law, which would include state authorization of local taxes. Existing local personal property taxes grandfathered.

I'm fairly convinced: the answer is NO.

Let me do one final check on the strongest pro-42 substantive argument to make sure I'm not missing something important — e.g., an argument from a tax policy expert (not funded by the campaign) that banning state wealth taxes is wise because of interstate competition. Jared Walczak (Tax Foundation) has written about Prop 40 being a bad idea. Let me check if Tax Foundation took a position on Prop 42. Quick search.

Not only has Gov.
Gavin Newsom vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax, but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future.
On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax.
Prop.
42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop.
40 passes.
But Prop.
42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property.
That includes pensions and 401K accounts before retirees start drawing retirement income from them.
It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax.

content.text:
**NO**

**What Prop 42 actually does** (Nov. 3, 2026 ballot): Amends the state Constitution to (1) ban any new state tax enacted on/after Jan. 1, 2026 on the "ownership or control" of personal property — defined to sweep in financial assets, retirement accounts, business interests, intellectual property, digital assets, vehicles, boats, art and "personal belongings" — and (2) ban retroactive taxes, including any tax keyed to past residency. It contains a poison‑pill clause nullifying Prop 40 (the billionaire wealth tax) if 42 gets more yes votes, plus unusual self‑entrenching provisions (mandatory independent counsel to defend it, a continuous General Fund appropriation, "liberal construction," revival if the rival measure is struck down).

**Why I land on no:**

1. **The stated rationale is a decoy.** The LAO confirms California does *not* tax ownership of financial assets, and no live proposal does. Prop 40 explicitly excludes qualified pensions and 401(k)s (only Roth-style accounts over $10M count); every one of the five recent legislative wealth-tax bills targeted people with $15M–$500M+ in assets. Any new state tax already requires a two‑thirds legislative vote or a majority vote of the people. The "protect your 401(k)" framing is misleading — which is precisely why McClatchy ("poison pill… 401(k) decoy"), the SF Chronicle, Press Democrat, Mercury News/East Bay Times, LA Times (Skelton), SPUR, the League of Women Voters and the California Democratic Party all say no.

2. **The ban is far broader than a wealth tax and permanent.** It would also foreclose future taxes on yachts/jets/art, intangible business property, digital assets, any new vehicle-license-fee-style charge (and state authorization of new local personal-property taxes), and tax-law professors Galle, Gamage and Shanske argue the loose drafting creates litigation risk for capital‑gains taxation, Prop 3's rate extension and VLF reform. Changing any of it later requires another statewide vote.

3. **The retroactivity ban is over-broad.** Voters approved Prop 30 (2012) with income-tax increases applied retroactively to Jan. 1, 2012 — a routine, court-sanctioned tool (and standard practice for year-start tax conformity and anti-avoidance). Prop 42's only carve-out is a ≤365-day legislative statute during a declared emergency; initiatives and legislative constitutional amendments get none.

4. **You don't need it to stop Prop 40.** Prop 40 is polling below 50% (Berkeley IGS 42–50; PPIC 46–52), and the Tax Foundation documents serious constitutional vulnerabilities in its retroactive Jan. 1 residency snapshot and intangible-property provisions. If you dislike the billionaire tax, just vote no on Prop 40 directly.

5. **Follow the money.** ~$128M for Prop 42, nearly all from Building a Better California, with Sergey Brin alone at $102M — the largest such intervention in state history, by people with a direct, enormous financial stake, sold to voters under a framing fact-checkers reject. Even Gov. Newsom, who endorses it, opposes the tax it targets on separate grounds.

The legitimate concern (a one-time retroactive 5% wealth tax invites capital flight and years of litigation) is a reason to vote **no on Prop 40** — not a reason to permanently constitutionalize a ban on taxing personal property and on retroactive taxation.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of
2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.
SEC. 4. Article VIII is added to the California
Constitution, to read:
ARTICLE VIII
SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,
Individually Owned Assets, and Other Forms of Personal
Savings
(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution
enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create,
impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership
or control of retirement holdings, individually owned
assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether
held directly or indirectly.
(b) Nothing in this section shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.
(c) Nothing in this section shall alter or affect the
taxation of real property as provided in other provisions
of this Constitution.
SEC. 2. Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
(a) (1) No state law and no provision of this
Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may
enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax
that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based
on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was
present prior to the effective date of the state law or
constitutional provision.
(2) This subdivision also applies to a tax that is imposed
on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a
date prior to the effective date of the tax.
(b) Nothing in subdivision (a) shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.

Let me now dig deeper into the substantive policy analysis. Key questions:

1. Does Prop 42 actually block Prop 40? Yes — via the conflicting measures provision and the retroactivity ban.
2. Is Prop 40 good policy? Consider: one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires residing in CA as of Jan 1, 2026. Estimated to raise ~$100B (LAO estimate?). Concerns: capital flight, valuation of private companies, legal challenges (dormant Commerce Clause, retroactivity, due process), and enforcement. Many economists and even progressive-leaning analysts have concerns. Newsom opposes. Several wealthy individuals have moved.
3. Is Prop 42 itself good policy independent of Prop 40? It permanently constitutionalizes a ban on new taxes on ownership of personal property — which could be over-broad and prevent future legislatures/voters from responding to new circumstances (e.g., AI-driven inequality, tax base erosion as economy shifts from labor income to capital). It also bans retroactive taxation, which while generally a good principle, could tie the state's hands in responding to federal changes or closing loopholes (though the measure carves out a limited exception for emergencies with a 365-day limit for statutes, not for initiatives? Let me re-read: Section 2(c) says subdivision (a) shall not apply to a tax imposed by a statute passed by the Legislature on or after Jan 1, 2026 where (1) not retroactive more than 365 days and (2) governor declares emergency... So there is a limited carve-out for legislative statutes in emergencies, but no carve-out for initiative measures — meaning voters could never enact a retroactive tax through initiative.

4. Is the claim about protecting retirement accounts truthful? There's no current proposal to tax middle-class retirement accounts; the LAO notes ownership of financial assets is not taxed. McClatchy calls it a "401(k) decoy." However, proponents argue it's preemptive protection requiring a vote of the people. Note that a constitutional amendment can itself only be changed by voters anyway — so the "protection" it provides is largely redundant with the two-thirds legislative vote requirement and the fact that any new state tax requires 2/3 legislative vote or ballot measure.

5. The measure includes an unusual "Legal Defense" provision that requires the AG to appoint independent counsel and creates a continuous General Fund appropriation. Also "Liberal Construction" clause. These provisions are designed to entrench.

6. Also, note the interaction: Prop 42's Section 1(a) prohibits "No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of..." — This could arguably affect other things, e.g., a future tax on business inventory? Business equipment personal property taxes are currently exempted by statute (there's a state subvention). Could block future taxes on intangible property.

Also, importantly — could Prop 42 block a future tax on, e.g., digital assets, or block a "mansion tax"? No, that's real property.

Another consideration: does Prop 42 potentially block local taxes? "No state law" — a local tax is enacted by local government, not state law, so probably not. But it could restrict the state from authorizing local personal property taxes.

Now — my job is to give a recommendation: yes or no. Let me gather more evidence: expert analysis (LAO, tax economists, legal scholars), and the campaign finance. Also check whether the "conflict" mechanism means voting yes on 42 kills Prop 40 — and whether Prop 40 has flaws severe enough.

Let me look at:
- LAO's fiscal estimate for Prop 40 (revenue estimates).
- Analysis by tax economists on the billionaire tax (e.g., David Gamage, who drafted it; critics like Jared Walczak of Tax Foundation).
- Legal challenges to Prop 40.
- Articles on how Prop 42 could backfire or its overbreadth (e.g., does it block taxes on unrealized gains at the state level; does it block a "personal property tax" needed to replace declining revenue).

Let me also see whether the two measures' conflict provision means that if Prop 40 passes with more votes, Prop 42 is void — so a "yes" on 42 only matters if 42 gets more yes votes than 40. That's important: voting yes on 42 while voting yes on 40 is coherent (a preference ranking). But the user asks about Prop 42 alone.

Let me research further.

Let me also weigh: Is there a legitimate fairness argument against retroactive taxation? Prop 40 applies to residency on Jan 1, 2026 — before voters approved it in Nov 2026. That is retroactive. Retroactive taxation is generally disfavored but often upheld if brief and justified (e.g., tax changes effective at start of tax year are common — many tax changes apply to the whole tax year even if enacted mid-year; e.g., California's 2012 Prop 30 raised income tax rates retroactively to Jan 1, 2012!). That's an important fact: Prop 30 (2012) applied retroactively to the beginning of the tax year. So a blanket constitutional ban on retroactivity could have prevented Prop 30-style measures — which are common tools to address mid-year fiscal shortfalls. So a future voter-approved initiative like Prop 30 (2012) — which was a legislative constitutional amendment, not an initiative — hmm, Prop 30 was placed on ballot by the Legislature. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic and disincentivize its further use by voting no.

Also — could Prop 42 bar a tax on the ownership of firearms? Ammunition tax is an excise tax on sale. A tax on gun ownership would be barred. Hmm, interesting but not central.

Also relevant: would Prop 42 prohibit a future state tax on cryptocurrency/digital assets ownership? Yes. Would it prohibit a state tax on stock ownership (like a mark-to-market tax on billionaires' unrealized gains — as NY and other states have considered)? A mark-to-market income tax is arguably a tax on income from unrealized appreciation, not on "ownership" — but it's based on ownership. Legal ambiguity here is a real concern: this ambiguity might chill future tax reforms even against high earners generally, e.g., California's proposal to tax unrealized gains (AB 1927? there was a proposal in 2025 to tax billionaires' unrealized gains). Actually there's the "2026 Billionaire Tax Act" plus proposals from Assemblymember Alex Lee for wealth taxes. Prop 42 would block all of them permanently unless repealed by voters.

Now, a key question for me as the assistant: what should the user vote? I need to come to a decision — yes or no — and provide reasoning. Let me weigh things carefully, and gather a bit more evidence, particularly:

1. Whether Prop 42's claims are misleading (401(k) protection). Verified: California doesn't tax retirement account ownership; Prop 40 excludes qualified retirement accounts and pensions; the "six proposals" claim — SF Chronicle says lawmakers killed all six wealth tax proposals since 2019; those targeted the rich, not 401(k)s. So the "protect your retirement" framing is largely a decoy.

2. Whether the retroactivity ban has independent merit. Retroactive taxation is disfavored, but modest retroactivity (to Jan 1 of the same year) is a common, legal legislative tool (e.g., Prop 30 in 2012, and tax changes effective retroactively to the start of the tax year). Prop 42's ban is absolute for initiatives, and for legislative statutes only allows up to 365 days in declared emergencies. This could hamper California's ability to conform to federal tax changes mid-year, or to close abusive tax shelters discovered mid-year. Actually many states enact retroactive conformity. The ban may create real fiscal-administration problems.

Hmm, wait. Let me re-read Section 2(a)(2): "This subdivision also applies to a tax that is imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." That's aimed at Prop 40.

3. Whether the measure entrenches itself via the Legal Defense provision (AG must appoint independent counsel with continuous General Fund appropriation). This is a notable governance red flag: it commandeers state funds and undermines the AG's authority, and it's designed to prevent the state from defending against it. Also the "liberal construction" instruction.

4. Whether it nullifies Prop 40 — yes, and this is a "poison pill" tactic. But note: such conflict provisions are common in CA initiative practice (e.g., Prop 22 in 2020 had a 7/8 amendment requirement; various measures). The LAO notes the conflict.

5. Consider the fairness/democracy angle: ~$293M-$368M from 30 billionaires to defeat Prop 40 and pass 41/42 — one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history. The measure is being sold to voters with a framing (protect your 401k) that is not accurate. Voting "no" rejects deceptive ballot-measure tactics.

6. On the other hand: is a state-level wealth tax actually bad policy? Evidence: wealth taxes have been abandoned across Europe (France, Sweden, etc.) due to capital flight and administration issues. California's income tax base is highly dependent on the ultra-wealthy (~top 1% pays ~45% of income tax; billionaires pay much). Even LAO warns of behavioral responses. Rauh/Jaros estimate net losses. Saez/Zucman estimate big revenue. Genuinely uncertain. But note: a NO vote on Prop 42 doesn't require endorsing Prop 40 — you can vote no on both. Since Prop 40 is polling below 50% and likely to fail on its own, the practical effect of voting no on 42 may be small — but if Prop 40 passes with fewer votes than 42, then 42 would kill it.

Hmm, but there's a strategic consideration: if you oppose Prop 40 and also oppose Prop 42, you vote no on both (like Mercury News and George Skelton). If you support Prop 40, you vote no on 42. The only people who should vote yes on 42 are those who want a permanent constitutional ban on personal property/wealth taxes and retroactive taxes.

So the real question: Should California permanently constitutionalize a ban on new taxes on ownership of personal property (including all intangible assets, business interests, IP, digital assets) and on retroactive taxation?

Considerations against a permanent ban:
- Tax policy needs flexibility. As the economy shifts (AI, capital vs labor income, decline of gas tax), states may need to tax wealth/capital. California's tax system is heavily reliant on income; a ban on personal property taxes forecloses a whole category.
- The measure's definition is extremely broad — "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including ... personal belongings." This could bar even modest, widely supported taxes like an annual luxury tax on private jets/yachts, or a tax on second homes' contents? Or a tax on stock/bond ownership.
- It's a one-way ratchet: it protects existing taxes (grandfather) but bars any new ones, even if approved by 2/3 of the Legislature or by a majority of voters (unless voters first repeal Prop 42). Actually — could voters approve a new wealth tax by initiative? Prop 42 says "No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact..." A later initiative that conflicts would need to expressly repeal/amend Prop 42 — under California law, an initiative can amend another initiative if it furthers its purpose or with voter approval; and constitutional amendments by voters can supersede. So it's not truly irreversible, but it raises the bar significantly (you'd need a separate repeal measure or a measure explicitly overriding).
- The measure's stated rationale is false/misleading (no proposal to tax 401(k)s; Prop 40 explicitly excludes qualified retirement accounts and pensions).
- Funded by parties with an enormous direct financial interest; the most expensive intervention in CA ballot history.

Considerations for:
- Retroactive taxation is genuinely disfavored; Prop 40's retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026 (before the election!) is a legitimate fairness concern. But Prop 42 goes much further.
- Wealth taxes are hard to administer and cause capital flight; banning them at state level could be seen as fiscal prudence (avoids a value-destroying one-time tax). But that's an argument for voting no on Prop 40, not for a permanent constitutional ban.
- Protecting pensions/retirement from future taxation: a real, if speculative, benefit. Note however that some argue there IS a plausible path: if a wealth tax on billionaires is enacted, expanding it to millionaires later is a known pattern ("boiling frog"). But the two-thirds requirement plus political reality makes it unlikely, and voters would have to approve.

Now let's check some more facts:
- Does Prop 40 exclude retirement accounts? The SF Chronicle says Prop 40 "specifically excludes qualified pensions and retirement accounts, including 401(k)s" but includes Roth IRAs over $10M as taxable assets. Let me verify from Prop 40's text. Actually LA Times says "Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded." And the Chronicle notes Roth IRAs >$10M included. So proponents of Prop 42's claim that Prop 40 would tax your retirement is mostly false (except mega-Roth IRAs which only billionaires have).
- Also the Yes on 42 campaign ads: did they claim Prop 40 would tax middle-class retirement accounts? SEIU says they spread lies. Let me check fact-checks of Prop 42 ads.

Also, check the "6 proposals to tax retirement and savings accounts" claim — SF Chronicle says lawmakers killed all six wealth tax proposals since 2019, none targeting 401(k)s. Let's see if any fact-check addressed the Prop 42 claim.

Let me also check whether Prop 42 would block the state's ability to tax, e.g., "control" — the phrase "ownership or control" could affect trust arrangements.

Additional angle: does Prop 42 possibly conflict with federal requirements or with the state's existing tax structure? Probably not.

Another important angle: Prop 42 could block a future tax on intangible personal property of businesses — which some states are considering as the economy digitizes. Also, could it block California from participating in a multistate approach to taxing digital assets? Yes.

Let me also see whether there is any analysis suggesting Prop 42 could affect the existing vehicle license fee or business personal property taxes if they were "re-enacted" — Section 1(b) says nothing alters taxes "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025." If the Legislature later amended the VLF rate, would that be a "new" tax? Ambiguity could create litigation risk over routine tax adjustments. For example, if the state increased the vehicle license fee, is that a "tax on ownership of personal property" enacted after Jan 1, 2026? Arguably yes — the VLF is a tax on ownership of vehicles (personal property)! So Prop 42 could bar any future increase in the vehicle license fee, or any new local/state tax on vehicles, boats, aircraft, business equipment. That's a much bigger deal than most voters realize: VLF increases have historically been used (and are a classic revenue tool). Also, the state could no longer replace declining gas-tax revenue with a road-charge or vehicle-based tax — a vehicle miles traveled (VMT) fee is arguably a fee, not a tax... but a VMT tax would be based on use, not ownership, so probably fine.

Hmm, but the ban is on taxes on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — as defined in Section 3(a) to include "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including... personal belongings". A VLF is a tax on ownership of a car (personal property) — so yes, Prop 42 would bar a new state tax on vehicle ownership. Wait — but is VLF a "tax"? Article XIII A Section 3(b)... hmm, VLF is actually an in-lieu property tax; it's in the Revenue & Taxation Code and is treated as a property tax. Actually, California's VLF is characterized as an ad valorem property tax on vehicles (personal property). So Prop 42 would prohibit new state VLF-type taxes. Also counties' business personal property taxes are local, not state, and existing.

That's a meaningful consequence: it forecloses taxing vehicles/boats/aircraft/business equipment — the classic personal property tax base — at the state level, and could also restrict the state's ability to authorize new local personal property taxes.

Also let me check the CalMatters article on Newsom's endorsement and any "what matters" explainer.

Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Newsom has not yet taken a position on Prop. 41, another Brin-backed, anti-billionaire tax measure that would nullify Prop. 40 by subjecting the tax revenues to certain state spending limits and audits, said spokesperson Izzy Gardon. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. Sign up for free Δ But he has also sought to take advantage this year of a populist upswing (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/) and frustration toward tech billionaires ahead of his decision on whether to run for president after he leaves office. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments.
